item.description: Netflix forecast fourth-quarter net income of $2.79 billion, below analyst expectations, and cut its 2026 advertising outlook to about $2.7 billion from $3 billion, sending shares down nearly 6% after hours. Third-quarter revenue rose 11.8% to $12.87 billion, its slowest growth in nearly three years, days after the company laid off about 6% of staff and replaced chief creative officer Bela Bajaria with Peter Rice. Co-CEO Ted Sarandos said, "I know that we could do better," adding that the company needs "better execution in the US."
item.dc:creator: Lisa Richwine and Jaspreet Singh, Reuters

item.title: United Airlines profit outlook well below estimates, hit by fuel costs
item.description: United Airlines forecast fourth-quarter adjusted earnings of 50 cents to $1.50 a share, a midpoint 43% below analyst estimates, as it expects to pay $4.80 a gallon for jet fuel despite record revenue and strong demand. Its extra fuel spending equaled nearly 70% of its quarterly revenue gain, narrowing its pretax margin to 6.2% from 8%, while Alaska Air Group projected a wider-than-expected fourth-quarter loss. With the Iran war threatening to keep fuel prices high into 2027, U.S. fares have already risen nearly 23% year over year, and Ryanair warned European fares could climb as much as 20% next year.
item.dc:creator: Rajesh Kumar Singh, Reuters

item.title: Kennedy says Trump administration aims for regulated market for peptides
item.description: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said the Trump administration wants a regulated marketplace for peptides, the amino-acid-chain compounds promoted on social media and by Kennedy himself despite scant evidence for their claimed uses. "Americans are going to be buying these anyway," he told Fox News, saying regulation would ensure products are what they claim and come from inspected factories. His remarks followed an FDA proposal sent to the White House that could make it easier for pharmacies to compound certain peptides, after outside advisers recommended loosening limits on six of seven under review against FDA staff guidance.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Utah attorney general sues 'prediction market' Kalshi over alleged illegal gambling
item.description: Utah Attorney General Derek Brown sued Kalshi in 3rd District Court, alleging the self-described prediction market is a gambling company and saying, "Kalshi runs an online casino in Utah and calls it a prediction market." The suit says about 80% to 90% of wagers on the platform involve sports, estimates Kalshi has collected $30.6 million to $61.2 million in fees from Utah accounts, and seeks restitution and injunctions. Kalshi, which is appealing a federal ruling that upheld Utah's gambling laws, says it is a federally regulated exchange and "no single state should have a veto over it."
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Weber State University reports record numbers in enrollment, degrees
item.description: Weber State University says it enrolled more than 33,000 students this fall and awarded more than 8,000 degrees and certificates last academic year, both records, crediting flexible degree pathways and programs that let high schoolers earn college credit. President Chris Mallett said, "We're here for all learners," and the school says more than 90% of its students come from Utah.
item.dc:creator: KSL Staff

item.title: Can larger batteries safely power residential buildings? A project in New York aims to show how
item.description: A 3.75 megawatt-hour lithium-ion battery at Buffalo's Peace Bridge Place affordable housing complex, among the largest in any U.S. residential building, will store power when it's plentiful and run the building when the grid is strained or down. Manufacturer Viridi spent six years and $10 million developing a container that isolates cells so one failure doesn't spread, and passed an indoor safety test that former DOE loan chief Jigar Shah called "near impossible." New York and California officials say distributed batteries can improve reliability and contain costs, with California adding 2,000 storage systems a week.
item.dc:creator: Jennifer McDermott, Associated Press

item.title: Salt Lake woman accused of trying to stab boy, burn him with hot pan
item.description: Prosecutors charged Alisha Ann Lucero, 43, with first-degree felony aggravated child abuse, alleging that in 2024 she held a hot pan near an 11-year-old boy's face and chased him with a kitchen knife in a stabbing motion at the home of the father of her children. According to charging documents, the boy said he believed she was trying to kill him and described earlier abuse, and both he and a sibling said they don't feel safe around her. Court records show Lucero, listed as transient, has a felony record dating to at least 2011, and it was unclear why charges came now.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Trump, Vance announce $25M whistleblower program to encourage reports of alleged fraud
item.description: President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance announced a $25 million Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program, run by the Justice Department, offering tipsters up to $30,000 when a tip leads to a fraud conviction or major enforcement action. Trump described the payments as a 1% commission and said he would personally settle competing claims: "I will be the arbitrator of all of these decisions." The event featured influencer Nick Shirley, whose video alleging fake Minnesota childcare centers drew the administration's attention, though a planned $10,000 check was not presented in front of reporters.
item.dc:creator: Darlene Superville, Associated Press

item.title: Genetic study shows seafarers from Easter Island settled Hawaii
item.description: A study in Science analyzing DNA from more than 1,000 Polynesians found Native Hawaiians are most closely related to the people of Easter Island, or Rapa Nui, pointing to Easter Islanders as Hawaii's first settlers after a voyage of more than 4,400 miles, likely in the 1200s. Co-senior author Keolu Fox of UC San Diego said Hawaii and Rapa Nui paired together in 61% of reconstructed family trees, a result so surprising the team "checked it four different ways." The researchers also say repeated founder effects concentrated rare variants linked to kidney disease and blindness in some Polynesian populations.
item.dc:creator: Will Dunham, Reuters

item.title: FAA clears the way for airlines to put Boeing's long-delayed 737 Max 10 into service
item.description: The FAA certified Boeing's 737 Max 10, the largest member of the 737 family, for passenger service after years of delays, with deliveries now expected in 2027 rather than the 2023 date Boeing once projected. More than 30 customers have ordered 1,555 undelivered Max 10s, over 30% of Boeing's 737 Max backlog, and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called the approval "a major win for American manufacturing." The plane, which typically seats 185 to 210 passengers, is Boeing's answer to Airbus's A321neo, and its certification completes the four-model Max lineup.
item.dc:creator: Josh Funk and Rio Yamat, Associated Press

item.title: Cornell rape accuser says president's response made her feel 'disbelieved'
item.description: The woman who has accused seven students of raping her at Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity house in 2024 wrote to faculty leaders that President Michael Kotlikoff questioned why she waited to report, according to a secondhand account from her sorority president, leaving her feeling "unsupported and disbelieved." Her Oct. 14 letter, sent as Jane Doe, arrives as the faculty Senate weighs a no-confidence resolution over what members call an "ongoing crisis" of campus sexual assault, with debate resuming Oct. 28. She said she was not telling faculty how to vote, and Kotlikoff did not immediately respond.
item.dc:creator: Leah Willingham, Associated Press

item.title: BYU freshman shares his improbable journey to a $3M field goal kick
item.description: BYU freshman Carter Smith described how he landed a $3 million field goal on ESPN's College GameDay after another student whose number was called lacked a physical ID. Smith, who mostly played soccer and had kicked maybe two field goals in his life, missed his first try in borrowed running shoes, then made the 33-yard kick barefoot with what he called a "knuckleball." He expects to owe at least $700,000 in taxes plus tithing and said the outcome was "honestly a miracle."
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: Zelenskyy says early warning system for Russian missile attacks resumed
item.description: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv is again receiving early warnings of Russian ballistic missile attacks after talks with U.S. officials including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who denied any policy change on intelligence or weapons and said, "Nothing has changed." Zelenskyy met U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo ahead of Witkoff's planned trip to St. Petersburg, as President Donald Trump pressed him to make a deal with Russia. Meanwhile, Russian missile and drone strikes killed at least nine people, and Zelenskyy said Ukraine has nearly run out of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors.
item.dc:creator: Hanna Arhirova and Barry Hatton, Associated Press

item.title: 2 men rearrested in UK on suspicion of assisting Iran over suspected plot at a US-run air base
item.description: British counterterrorism police rearrested two men, ages 24 and 25, under the National Security Act on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service in a suspected Sept. 27 plot at RAF Fairford, a U.S.-run base used in bombing Iran. Police found gasoline in three vans but no explosives, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the plot was "almost certainly" directed by Iran's Revolutionary Guard, which Iran denies. No one has been charged, and MI5 chief Ken McCallum says more than 50 people have been arrested over Iran-linked plots in the past year.
item.dc:creator: Sylvia Hui, Associated Press

item.title: At least $963K in trading cards were stolen from a FedEx truck in California
item.description: Santa Ana police are investigating the Oct. 13 theft of at least $963,000 in Pokémon and sports trading cards from an unattended FedEx truck outside Professional Sports Authenticator, the grading company known as PSA. Two pallets were taken, and PSA's parent company, Collectors, said it deactivated the stolen cards' certificates, alerted marketplaces and arranged fair-market compensation for affected customers. Boston-area collector Nick Andrews told the AP collectors' true losses likely run to "millions of dollars, most likely."
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: Flood watches issued in Utah as state's stormy October continues
item.description: The National Weather Service issued flood watches across much of southern and central Utah from Wednesday morning through Thursday evening, warning that localized rainfall of 2 to 3 inches could cause flash flooding in slot canyons, slickrock areas and burn scars. KSL meteorologist Matt Johnson said a low-pressure system will bring waves of storms south of I-70 first before splitting over the state, with the Wasatch Front and northern Utah collecting up to an inch or more by early Saturday and 3 to 6 inches of snow possible above 8,500 feet. The rain could push mountain soil moisture, already at record mid-October levels after Tropical Storm Rachel's remnants, to the highest for meteorological fall since records began in 2006.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Feared extinct, Bangka slow loris primate rediscovered in Indonesia
item.description: The Bangka slow loris, a venomous nocturnal primate last scientifically documented between 1930 and 1932 and listed by the IUCN as possibly extinct, has been confirmed alive on Indonesia's Bangka island, according to a study in the journal Spixiana. The Alobi Wildlife Rescue Center documented more than 90 of the animals across the island from 2015 to 2025 and released 86 into the wild, many after rescues from homes and plantations or injuries from electrical wires. Co-author Timon Glaw urged protecting the island's remaining forests from tin mining and oil palm expansion, saying losing the species "would mean losing something truly irreplaceable."
item.dc:creator: Will Dunham, Reuters

item.title: Early flu season, current strain may signal risk for younger people; doctors urge shots
item.description: Doctors are urging flu shots for everyone 6 months and older after an unusually early rise in cases on the West Coast, where 10.7% of lab tests came back positive last week versus 0.5% a year earlier. This season's dominant H1N1 strain carries a new G155E mutation that antibodies from teens and young adults did not recognize in small studies, raising worries it "may be more severe" in younger people, said Mount Sinai's Dr. Jennifer Duchon. Vaccination has slipped, with about 58 million adults getting shots last season, and experts including Paul Offit blame reduced federal promotion under Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
item.dc:creator: Michael Erman and Julie Steenhuysen, Reuters

item.title: 2 people hit, critically injured by truck in West Valley City
item.description: A 39-year-old man and a 37-year-old woman were hospitalized in critical condition, though reportedly awake and talking, after a truck struck them as they crossed Redwood Road near 2495 South in West Valley City around 1:09 a.m. Tuesday. Police spokeswoman Roxeanne Vainuku said the 54-year-old driver, who reported going through a green light when the pair ran into the road, stayed at the scene and showed no sign of intoxication.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: New Utah dinosaur dig marks end of an era
item.description: Utah Geological Survey paleontologists have begun excavating the Ironstone Bonebed north of Arches National Park, among the oldest Cretaceous sites in North America, which could shed light on what followed the extinction event at the end of the Jurassic. State paleontologist Jim Kirkland says it already holds four kinds of dinosaur and will take "decades of work," and it appears to include a new armored species he plans to name for longtime colleague Don DeBlieux. DeBlieux, who has found more than 500 fossil localities in Utah and has worked beside Kirkland for 25 years, retires from the survey at year's end but calls it "more of a transition."
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: Driver allegedly looking up porn charged in fatal I-15 crash
item.description: Prosecutors charged Christine Chao, 44, of Rosemead, California, with second-degree felony automobile homicide in a June 12 crash in a construction zone on northbound I-15 near Levan that killed 66-year-old Scott LaVar Lichfield of Fillmore. Charging documents say a warrant search of her phone showed she had accessed a pornography website less than two minutes before she rear-ended slowed traffic without leaving brake marks. Lichfield's obituary says he had just marked his 39th wedding anniversary and loved playing Santa Claus for children.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Utah sees rise in unaffiliated voters as dissatisfaction grows
item.description: Consultant Taylor Morgan of Morgan and May Public Affairs urges disaffected Utah voters to join a major party and reshape it from within rather than leave, warning that departures by moderates and voters aged 18 to 35 will make both parties more extreme. His advice comes as state elections data shows about 30,000 more unaffiliated voters than a year ago, a shift Morgan describes as moving "from red and blue to none of the above." He also said politicians could reverse the trend by working across the aisle instead of playing only to their base.
item.dc:creator: Heather Peterson, KSL

item.title: Is the US doing enough to help Ukraine? 'No,' Utah senator says
item.description: Asked whether the U.S. is doing enough to help Ukraine, Sen. John Curtis said bluntly, "No," criticizing President Donald Trump's Russian diesel deal as cash Russia would use to recruit soldiers and prolong the war. Curtis, who visited Kyiv and Kharkiv last month, rejected Trump's rationale for pausing new sanctions, arguing that Russia comes to the table because it is running out of resources, and framed the war as "good versus evil." The story contrasts his view with Mitt Romney's weekend warning and Sen. Mike Lee's opposition to more Ukraine funding.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko and Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: A unicorn villain, Dolly Parton and skeletal headgear lead Google's 2026 costume searches
item.description: Google Trends' annual Frightgeist report puts Buddy the Unicorn, the villain from the horror comedy "Buddy," atop national costume searches, followed by the viral NeeDoh squishy toy, while Salt Lake's list is led by the Grinch, the Grim Reaper and an angel. Dolly Parton ranks high for both pet and kids' costumes, which Google's Megan Stoner said points to "a Western pop star Halloween." Candy Corn remains the most-searched candy for a fifth straight year, and searches for crockpot cauldrons and Santa hats sized for 12-foot skeletons have hit new highs.
item.dc:creator: Simone Seikaly, KSL

item.title: Mitt Romney issues rare statement as Republicans challenge Trump's Russia deal
item.description: Former Utah Sen. Mitt Romney posted a rare public warning against trading away Ukraine, loosely quoting John F. Kennedy and writing, "Abandon Ukraine and we abandon liberty." His post followed President Donald Trump's executive order exempting Russia from a sanctions package Congress passed last month, a week after Trump announced a deal to import Russian diesel. Some Republicans, including retiring Rep. Don Bacon, have threatened to stall Trump's lame-duck agenda over the move, while Trump says he doesn't want to drive Russia away from peace talks.
item.dc:creator: Cami Mondeaux, Deseret News

item.title: Ecuadorean man decries detention, second immigration arrest involving Ogden police officers
item.description: Dennys Alcivar Torres, an Ecuadorean man detained by ICE agents in an Ogden parking lot on Sept. 3 with help from an Ogden police officer, told the City Council his arrest was a physical attack and asked that police accept reports from people alleging abuse by ICE. His case is the second involving Ogden officers that immigrant advocates cite in pressing for a department policy on ICE interactions; police say they are reviewing the incident and working on such a policy. Alcivar says he was legally pursuing a student visa, while the Department of Homeland Security says his application was denied for abandonment and that he resisted arrest.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: 'Going strong': Farr's Jewelry, born of a family with deep roots in Ogden, marks its 70th year
item.description: Farr's Jewelry in Ogden marked 70 years Monday with a ribbon-cutting, a milestone general manager Mike Ash called "a pretty incredible run" for a store best known for wedding rings. Founded in 1956 by Vern Farr Jr., who still owns it at 98, the business descends from Lorin Farr, Ogden's first mayor, though it is separate from the family's Farr Better Ice Cream. Vice president Dirk Farr said shoppers still want to touch and try on jewelry in person, and Ash said the store now sells rings to the grandchildren of 1950s and '60s customers.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Payson woman fights for coverage after health plan drops her provider, leaving her with $13K bill
item.description: Payson resident Jennifer Rieske had a prior authorization letter for her April surgery but was billed more than $13,600 as out-of-network after Florida Blue dropped the hospital from its network on April 1, a day after approving coverage and 15 days before the operation. The KSL Investigators pointed to the No Surprises Act's "continuity of care" provision, which can let some patients keep in-network terms for up to 90 days after a provider leaves their plan. After KSL contacted the insurer, Florida Blue approved billing her surgery as in-network; the story notes patients must apply for continuity of care themselves.
item.dc:creator: Matt Gephardt and Sloan Schrage, KSL

item.title: Invasive 'yellow fever mosquito' found in Davis County for the first time
item.description: An Aedes aegypti, or "yellow fever mosquito," turned up during routine surveillance at Clearfield's Bicentennial Park on Oct. 8, the first time the invasive species has been found in Davis County after being routinely detected in southern Utah since 2019. The daytime-biting mosquito can carry Zika, dengue and yellow fever and breeds in small amounts of standing water, though extra trapping hasn't found more and will continue until cold weather arrives. Health department director Brian Hatch said its presence raises the possibility that diseases now tied to travel "could become locally transmitted."
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Vaccine interest rises as US measles cases reach 35-year high
item.description: Confirmed U.S. measles cases reached 4,080 as of Oct. 8, a 35-year high, with Pennsylvania, Utah and South Carolina hosting the largest outbreaks and at least six reported deaths, though the CDC officially counts two after HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. changed how measles deaths are classified. Utah has confirmed 527 cases in 2025-2026, many in the Southwest Utah health district. TriCounty Health Department's Kirk Benge said keeping unvaccinated students home helped end an outbreak there and that MMR shots for children rose 500% between March 2025 and March 2026.
item.dc:creator: Lois M. Collins, Deseret News

item.title: Utah colleges prepare for enrollment plateau after years of growth
item.description: After five years of record growth, the University of Utah is preparing for enrollment to level off, as the Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute projects Utah's 18-to-24 population will peak around 2028 and then fall about 18% before rebounding around 2047. U. communications director Rebecca Walsh said the state's schools are coordinating so they avoid "cannibalizing each other's programs," steering students toward the programs that best fit them and emphasizing degrees that lead quickly to jobs.
item.dc:creator: Adam Small, KSL

item.title: Tremonton husband accused of recruiting man to break in, rape his wife
item.description: Tremonton man Jeremiah West and Noel Ayala, 49, face first-degree felony charges after police say West recruited Ayala to break into his home and rape his wife, falsely telling him she had a "fantasy" of it and should not know he arranged it. Charges say West let Ayala in early on Sept. 13 and Ayala attacked the woman in her bed before her 15-year-old son helped chase him out. Investigators also allege West sold intimate photos of his wife, made AI-altered explicit images of her and her sister, and raped her the day before; she told police she knew nothing of the scheme.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: USU uses Roblox and Minecraft to reach potential students in the virtual world
item.description: Utah State University professors and students are building virtual versions of campus in Roblox and Minecraft to reach prospective students, with the Roblox "Aggie Campus Life" game currently covering the quad and Taggart Student Center. Professor Ramy Shaaban, who redesigned a course around Roblox, said "Roblox is a perfect tool for Gen Alpha," and players can earn in-game Aggie Bucks by attending classes and activities. The Roblox project is in beta ahead of a 1.0 launch called "Light the A" in February, while the Minecraft build targets older teens and college students.
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: 3 Utah universities among best places to get a technology degree
item.description: A study by tech firm Ajelix ranking 514 U.S. institutions on tech graduate earnings, debt, net price, retention and accreditation placed three Utah schools in its top 25, led by BYU at No. 3 behind the University of Illinois and MIT. BYU grads reported earning $130,543 four years out with median federal debt of $11,178, while 11th-ranked Utah Valley University had the lowest average net price in the top 25 at $6,376. The University of Utah ranked 22nd, with tech graduates earning a reported $124,517, as it launches a new bachelor's degree in artificial intelligence.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Norway targets 'harmful' social media, games with under-16 ban
item.description: Norway said its planned ban on social media for children under 16 will target "harmful platforms," and that the government believes TikTok, Roblox and Snapchat will be covered. Children and Families Minister Lene Vaagslid said the bill addresses risks from harmful content and addictive features to unwanted contact from strangers, and makes tech companies responsible for age verification. The bill, due before parliament by year's end, follows Australia's first-in-the-world under-16 ban, while messaging services and games deemed harmless will remain open to children.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Rental demand increases as cost of homeownership keeps rising
item.description: Zillow data show homebuying costs rising nearly twice as fast as rent, with a typical $3,037 monthly owner payment versus $1,932 to rent, and Utah single-family homes costing about $4,000 a month to own versus $2,500 to rent, per the Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute. Gardner analyst Dejan Eskic said mortgage rates rising from about 6% to 7.4% have added $400 to $450 a month for new buyers, while Zillow economist Kara Ng described "the rise of the deliberate renter." Rental demand rose 7.4% in the Salt Lake area, though a glut of new apartments has pushed Wasatch Front apartment rents about 8% below their peak.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Musk, Anthropic outline dueling approaches to AI-era philanthropy
item.description: Anthropic said it will commit 5% of its shares, potentially worth $75 billion to $100 billion at a planned IPO valuation, to a new Public Benefit Fund that could make direct distributions and address AI's effect on jobs, while Elon Musk pledged to give one SpaceX share to "every kid in America," a gift worth roughly $11 billion. Musk argued that giving shares "directly to the people is the way," and President Trump thanked him in connection with the Trump Accounts program, though one portfolio manager called it "a publicity stunt." Anthropic said the fund's equity won't be used for lobbying or political giving and that, with founder pledges and employee matching, about 20% of its shares will go to public purposes.
item.dc:creator: Deborah Mary Sophia and Abu Sultan, Reuters

item.title: Mississippi AG says officer's force was justified during shoplifting call in which boy was killed
item.description: Mississippi's attorney general concluded that a Senatobia police officer was justified in using force in the June shooting that killed 1-year-old Kohen Wiley as officers responded to a shoplifting call at a Walmart. Authorities said the car carrying Kohen and his mother drove toward officers, but his mother denied that and any theft, and family attorney Ben Crump has said an independent autopsy indicates Kohen was shot from the side of the car. The case adds to strained relations between the department and Senatobia's Black residents, including the recent firing of the former police chief over alleged racist texts.
item.dc:creator: Sophie Bates, Associated Press

item.title: 'Y'all ready to die?' man with machete allegedly asks teens before robbing them
item.description: Anthony Ray Turnbow, 18, was charged with aggravated robbery and aggravated assault after allegedly brandishing a machete at six teenage boys walking home from basketball near 1500 West and 600 South in Salt Lake City, asking, "Y'all ready to die?" Charging documents say he chased the group, then found two boys hiding in a backyard, forced them to their knees, took their wallets and assaulted them, causing minor injuries. Police said his threats could be heard on the boys' 911 call and are investigating whether he had any prior history with them.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Marine life dramatically declined in Gulf of Mexico in years after BP oil spill, study finds
item.description: A new study found that marine life in the Gulf of Mexico's deep "twilight zone" fell by about 60% in the years after the 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill, with fish down 63.5%, crustaceans 62% and krill 72%, and populations still not recovered. Lead author Tracey Sutton of Nova Southeastern University said temperature, oxygen and food did not track the decline, leaving the spill as the most likely cause, and genetic tests showed species losing diversity. Outside scientists called the result alarming, with Dalhousie's Boris Worm citing "little visible recovery" after 13 years and urging caution about deep-sea mining and drilling.
item.dc:creator: Seth Borenstein, Associated Press

item.title: Nvidia-backed Nscale, Anthropic in talks for new $45 billion AI cloud deal, source says
item.description: Data center developer Nscale is negotiating a new deal worth about $45 billion to sell AI computing power to Anthropic from a second building at its Monarch campus in West Virginia, which would supply 460 megawatts using Nvidia Vera Rubin chips, a source told Reuters. It would follow Anthropic's $45 billion agreement in August for Nscale's first West Virginia facility, and Anthropic also holds a right of first refusal on a third building. The talks come after Microsoft withdrew from anchoring a flagship Nscale data center over power delays and as investors scrutinize debt-funded AI infrastructure following a selloff led by CoreWeave.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Have You Seen This? Highland cows 'Stayin' Alive'
item.description: In her "Have You Seen This?" column, Arianne Brown shares a social media clip of shaggy Highland cows strutting to the Bee Gees' "Stayin' Alive," recalling that she first doubted the breed was real after spotting a photo at her dentist's office. Her feed has since steered her to a Spanish Fork farm that offers "cow cuddles" with the animals, and she now considers them "1970s disco stars incarnate."
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Exclusive-How one hacker used AI agents and a few thousand dollars to break into scores of sites
item.description: NorForge researcher Snorre Fagerland told Reuters that a Chinese-speaking hacker used AI agents running on exposed instances of the open-source Cairn platform to break into websites of more than 100 companies, including Deere, SharkNinja and Cummins, with almost no human effort. The agents attempted more than 1,200 sites from terse instructions, with successful intrusions typically taking about 23 hours, and Fagerland said some techniques were "not script kiddie stuff." Deere and SharkNinja said the incidents were remediated or contained, and Cairn's author said the tool "was not designed for hacking attacks."
item.dc:creator: Raphael Satter, Reuters

item.title: Trump's trade adviser defends tariffs, touts Texas Instrument investment in new Lehi plant
item.description: Touring Texas Instruments' $11 billion semiconductor plant under construction in Lehi, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer defended Trump administration tariffs as "leveling the playing field" against subsidized foreign competitors and said they protect jobs. With consumer prices up about 3.7% annually, driven partly by gas, Greer argued food staples like beef and bananas aren't tariffed and that any tariff price effect is a "one-time" bump, though a New York Fed study found tariffs raised prices on 67 types of goods. The plant is expected to add 800 high-paying jobs and strengthen domestic chip supply.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: 1 seriously wounded, another arrested after shooting triggers school lockdown in West Valley City
item.description: A boy was seriously wounded in a shooting near 1142 S. 2320 South in West Valley City on Monday afternoon, prompting a lockdown at nearby Roots Charter High School. Police later found the suspected gun and arrested one person at a Salt Lake City TRAX station, and said they believe there is no ongoing threat to the public.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Australian prime minister says lawmaker critically injured by car is 'no accident'
item.description: Independent Australian lawmaker Helen Haines, 65, was critically injured when a Toyota Land Cruiser struck her outside her electoral office in Wangaratta, Victoria, and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said "this wasn't an accident." A passerby detained the 43-year-old driver, police found a knife in the vehicle, and the national counterterrorism team is investigating, though police called it an isolated incident. The attack renewed concern over lawmaker safety, with Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke citing more than 1,000 threats against politicians in the last financial year and Albanese blaming a polarized climate fueled partly by social media.
item.dc:creator: Rod McGuirk and Charlotte Graham-McLay, Associated Press

item.title: Man accused of throwing rocks at passing cars on US-6
item.description: Nicholas Sean-Leo Proulx, 37, of Salt Lake City, was arrested at gunpoint after police said he jumped in front of cars and threw rocks, including one a driver called a "boulder," at vehicles on U.S. 6 near Silver Summit, cracking a windshield and denting another car. Officers called off a drone-assisted search near the Utah-Wasatch county line, but a man then flagged down a departing trooper, disappeared and reappeared shouting on the road shoulder. He was booked for investigation of criminal mischief, reckless endangerment and aggravated disorderly conduct about 90 minutes after the first 911 call.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: US banning Chinese AI DeepSeek from government agency IT systems
item.description: The Department of Homeland Security ordered civilian federal agencies to remove DeepSeek products and third-party services built on the Chinese AI model from their IT systems and barred agencies from acquiring them. DHS said the models pose "multiple threat vectors," could send sensitive data to China and may contain malware. The move follows earlier DeepSeek bans by the Commerce Department, the Navy and states such as New York and Virginia, amid a wider administration crackdown that includes an Oct. 29 FCC vote to bar Chinese labs from testing U.S. electronics.
item.dc:creator: David Shepardson, Reuters

item.title: $105M fund launched for new Yellowstone National Park infrastructure, education
item.description: The National Park Service announced a $105 million fund with Blackstone subsidiary Tallgrass Energy Partners and Yellowstone Forever for stewardship, visitor infrastructure and education at Yellowstone, with a $35 million Norris Geyser Basin visitor center among the projects under consideration. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum likened it to Theodore Roosevelt's efforts to expand access, and the park service will keep control of how the money is spent. The deal comes after 45 Yellowstone maintenance projects and 51 at Utah parks were reportedly moved to a low-priority list, which a Center for Western Priorities staffer said covered "the basic work national parks need to function."
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Utah's LG says Postal inspector intercepted letter with suspicious powder meant for her office
item.description: A U.S. postal inspector intercepted an envelope containing "suspicious white powder and threatening letters" addressed to Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson's office and handed it to the FBI, one of several such mailings sent to election officials and congressional offices ahead of the midterms. Henderson said powder in similar letters was non-toxic, "just a scare tactic," and vowed that nothing would disrupt the election. She received a similar letter in 2024 and has resisted Justice Department requests for Utah's full voter rolls, which she says state law bars her from providing.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Teen Memoriam honors 30 teens killed in Utah crashes in 2025
item.description: The annual Zero Fatalities Teen Memoriam honors the 30 teens killed on Utah roads in 2025, a year in which 43 teen drivers were involved in fatal crashes that killed 47 people, with speeding and reckless driving blamed for most. Families shared their losses to warn young drivers, including the parents of Branson Davis, killed in a motorcycle crash, and Rob Wilson, whose 17-year-old daughter Anneka was killed by a wrong-way drunk driver. Released during National Teen Driver Safety Week, the publication is shared with Utah schools, and Wilson urged families to "hug them, hold them tight — even if you're mad."
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: The winners and losers of Utah's record-warm 2026 water year
item.description: Utah's 2026 water year, which ended Sept. 30, was the warmest on record by 2.1 degrees, and although mountain precipitation reached 96% of normal, snowpack barely topped 50%, leaving reservoirs at 48% of capacity and the whole state in at least moderate drought. Federal data showed Rich and Cache counties among the precipitation winners, while Millard, Juab, Tooele and Salt Lake counties fared worst. Remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel gave the 2027 water year record soil moisture, but Utah Snow Survey director Jordan Clayton said, "We don't want to hang our hat on having an above-normal winter just yet."
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Attorney representing Kouri Richins on fraud charges asks to withdraw
item.description: Attorney Amy Fowler asked to withdraw from Kouri Richins' fraud and forgery case, citing a "breakdown of communication," after Richins wrote the court alleging Fowler had represented a key witness in her murder trial and has close ties to the judge and a prosecutor. Judge Richard Mrazik said he would grant the request only once new counsel is assigned, saying he can't leave Richins unrepresented, and set a Nov. 6 hearing. Richins, already serving life without parole for murdering her husband, Eric, faces 26 felony counts including mortgage fraud and money laundering.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Who is responsible when AI causes harm?
item.description: At a Utah Valley University summit on regulating artificial intelligence hosted by Rep. Celeste Maloy, AI Ethics and Governance Institute director Medlir Mema likened AI to a "gray rhino" that is predictable but moves deceptively fast. Panelists credited Utah's Office of AI Policy and its regulatory sandbox, which grants companies temporary relief while they pilot products, and Gov. Spencer Cox's Pro-Human Initiative, while Clarion AI Partners CEO Bennett Borden argued liability now falls on deployers rather than model developers. Deputy Attorney General Stewart Young said regulation alone won't rein in companies with "trillions of dollars" and urged states to strengthen criminal law.
item.dc:creator: Leah Bowers, Deseret News

item.title: Report: Utah gets strong financial grade despite 'repeated problems' handling federal funds
item.description: Truth in Accounting ranked Utah fourth among the states for financial health and gave it an "A," citing a $17.2 billion cushion at the end of fiscal 2025, or a $14,900 surplus per taxpayer. Jeff Moss of the Governor's Office of Economic Opportunity said strong finances help states weather downturns and pay for schools and roads. The same report flagged a federal Single Audit that found "repeated problems" in how state agencies handled the $11.6 billion in federal grants Utah received in 2025, including unsupported records, late reimbursements and contractor overcharges.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: A rare family of barn owls moved into Manhattan's Upper West Side. New Yorkers are captivated
item.description: A family of barn owls nesting in a water tower on West 75th Street near Central Park is believed to be the first documented barn owl nest in Manhattan's recorded history, drawing nightly crowds of birders and photographers. Manhattan Bird Alert's David Barrett has counted at least one adult and five fledglings, and neighbors described weeks of nighttime screeching that one man said sounded like someone "being murdered outside." Barn owls are rare in New York, at the northern edge of their range, and resident Elisabeth Williams, who first reported them, said, "I think we're about to become birders."
item.dc:creator: Joseph Frederick and Josh Kelety, Associated Press

item.title: US company announces progress toward resurrecting the extinct dodo
item.description: Dallas-based Colossal Biosciences said a new AI platform called GenoMorph has narrowed the genetic changes behind the dodo's distinctive beak and skull to about 2,300 candidates, as it works to edit dodo traits into its closest living relative, the Nicobar pigeon. The company said its dodo genome is 95% complete and its Texas pigeon colony has grown to 36 birds, but it gave no timeline for hatching a dodo. CEO Ben Lamm said the remaining hurdles include proving which edits matter and preparing Mauritius by removing invasive predators, adding that bringing the bird back "shows extinction doesn't have to be permanent."
item.dc:creator: Will Dunham, Reuters

item.title: Utah Tech adds clinical psychology, counseling master's in effort to expand mental health access
item.description: Utah Tech University will launch a master's program in counseling and clinical psychology in fall 2027 with 18 spots, aiming to ease a shortage of mental health professionals in southern and rural Utah, where suicide rates have stayed higher than in cities. Program director Lisa Scott said many aspiring therapists in the area have few options beyond online training, and about 90% of the school's psychology students said they were interested. Students will provide closely supervised, low-cost care at a new community clinic, and the school plans to seek American Psychological Association accreditation, which only six master's programs nationwide now hold.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Westminster Dog Show taps Utahn as agility judge
item.description: Tracy Mazur, a Cocker spaniel trainer who also works for Canyons School District's preschool department, will become Utah's first agility judge at the Westminster Kennel Club Dog Show, a call she first suspected was spam or a prank. She'll design and judge the agility course at New York's Javits Center, with the championship set for Jan. 30, 2027, ahead of the purebred competition at Madison Square Garden. Mazur, who grew up in a dog-rescuing Wisconsin family, said trust is the key to the dog-handler bond and that "in the dog world, this is about as big as it gets."
item.dc:creator: Lee Benson, Deseret News

item.title: Smith's Ballpark transforms into international climbing venue
item.description: USA Climbing turned Smith's Ballpark, the former home of the Salt Lake Bees, into the venue for the final stop of the 2026 World Climbing Series, bringing about 160 athletes from 35 countries for three days of bouldering with baseball-themed touches like jerseys. CEO Marc Norman said the empty stadium was a chance "to lean into America's pastime," and more than 8,000 tickets sold, over 70% to out-of-state buyers. Competitor Sovarae Sanders said she was "losing my mind" seeing the fans when she walked out to climb.
item.dc:creator: Tyrese Boone, KSL

item.title: Utah-based initiative connecting families with local resources for special needs children
item.description: The CHILL Act Expo, a nonprofit that gathers providers for children with special needs in one free event for families, wrapped up its fourth Utah expo of 2026 in Logan. Director Amit Lodha said in-person contact reveals options families miss online, recalling parents who drove 30 miles for therapy without knowing a provider was a mile from home. He said the expos have served 6,000 parents and 700 providers this year and offered more than 250 free autism pre-screenings, with more Utah events planned for 2027.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Earnshaw, KSL

item.title: Utah man walks across Japan in more than 100 days for Asthma awareness
item.description: Holladay's Will Richards quit his job and spent 118 days walking the length of Japan, from Cape Soya to Cape Sata, often camping by the road, to raise awareness of asthma after his father, John, died suddenly of an acute asthma attack five years ago. The route passed through areas where his father served a Latter-day Saint mission, and about 90 days in, his grandfather and a cousin secretly flew out to join him, revealing themselves during a family video prayer. Richards has since started a foundation and the Kickin' Asthma Half Marathon at Deer Creek Reservoir, set for Oct. 24.
item.dc:creator: Erin Cox, KSL

item.title: Charter school planned near Mapleton public elementary sparks concerns over traffic, safety
item.description: The planned Louisa May Alcott Community School, a publicly funded charter built around outdoor, place-based learning for 525 students in kindergarten through seventh grade, has drawn opposition for its site across the street from Mapleton's Hobble Creek Elementary. Neighbors such as Jen Sommerfeldt have organized petitions over traffic on a narrow street without consistent sidewalks, and Nebo School District Superintendent Rick Nielsen asked the city to delay approvals, calling a second school beside an under-capacity one "an illogical and questionable use of taxpayer dollars." Clint Biesinger of Roundtable Funding said the school is planning staggered start times and carpools, and it hopes to open for the 2027-28 school year; the city says state law limits its role.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Electric guitar serenade aims to deter dumpster-diving black bears
item.description: Andy M. Phail of western North Carolina went viral after a video showed him playing electric guitar on his porch to drive off black bears raiding a dumpster, a week after the same bears broke into his Jeep and ate five chocolate cakes. He said he turned to music as "the only thing I know to use in life to help a rough situation get better," and noted that his late mother appears in the Instagram video. North Carolina wildlife officials warn that bears fed by trash, pet food or birdseed lose their fear of people and urge residents to secure garbage and remove feeders.
item.dc:creator: Ruby Annas, WLOS

item.title: Pope Leo tells faithful in St. Peter's Square he will gradually resume duties after cancer surgery
item.description: Speaking from his window at the Sunday Angelus four days after surgery to remove a malignant lung tumor, Pope Leo XIV thanked cheering crowds in St. Peter's Square and said he would "gradually resume my activities." He said the week had made him feel close to those facing illness, and pilgrims, including Americans eager to pray with the first U.S.-born pope, described the quick recovery as a relief. Tests on the tumor and lymph nodes will determine whether he needs chemotherapy, immunotherapy or targeted therapy, while his surgeon sees no clinical obstacle to the planned Nov. 6-17 South America trip.
item.dc:creator: Colleen Barry and Trisha Thomas, Associated Press

item.title: Fifth oldest Lutheran church west of Rocky Mountains honors Swedish heritage
item.description: Salt Lake City's Zion Evangelical Lutheran Church, founded in 1882 by five Swedish immigrants and now the fifth-oldest Lutheran church west of the Rockies, has moved from a sod hut to a downtown building to its 1957 "Swedish Modern" home near Foothill Drive. Unofficial historian Paul Mogren described artifacts that survived the moves, including a bell from Sweden that a custodian's son nearly sold for scrap in the 1940s and a 1905 painting, "The Consoling Christ," that turned up at an estate sale in 2024 and was restored in 2025. Swedish services ended by the mid-1930s, and the congregation now runs music camps with waiting lists and tries "to be as open as we possibly can."
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Young adults involved in 'Dedicate' now sharing their experiences around the world
item.description: Young adults featured in "Dedicate," the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints' weekly series on the renovated Salt Lake Temple, have been speaking at local screenings in Brazil, France and elsewhere ahead of the 2027 Temple Celebration. Episodes show the seven participants meeting church leaders, learning how 98 base isolators and vertical cables protect the temple from earthquakes, and helping with construction; Sora Murata said base isolation represents faith because "we can always come back." Elder Gary E. Stevenson said the series lets those who can't attend in person take part, with episodes releasing weekly through Nov. 1 in 12 languages and a finale in spring 2027.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Orem Chinese-immersion students help welcome President Xi to US
item.description: Orem High students Abigail Clark and Teon Sonomura, whose fourth-grade Chinese immersion class received a reply letter from President Xi Jinping in 2020, joined an 18-person Utah delegation organized by BYU professor Peter Chan to welcome Xi to Washington. The group gave Chinese diplomats a Utah-China Friendship Quilt honoring Chinese railroad workers and a letter inviting Xi to Utah; when his motorcade took another exit, reporters interviewed the students instead. Both, who visited China on an embassy scholarship last spring, now help Chan recruit exchange students, and Teon said, "Both nations are great and we underestimate each other."
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: 2nd annual Resource Fair offers free Naloxone kits
item.description: The Salt Lake County Health Department held its second annual Resource Fair, offering free naloxone kits along with disease and mental health screenings and hygiene kits to raise awareness of services already available. Health educator coordinator Ayan Nor called naloxone "just as important as knowing how to do CPR," noting that even people prescribed opioids face overdose risk. Opioid prescriptions in Utah have fallen since 2022, but state data show 244 opioid overdose deaths in 2026, and county clinics continue to hand out kits for free.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Earnshaw, KSL

item.title: Pope Leo XIV returns to Vatican 4 days after cancer surgery
item.description: Pope Leo XIV left Rome's Gemelli Hospital and returned to the Vatican four days after surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, where lung adenocarcinoma was found, walking unaided and telling friars he hoped to meet again "not for these reasons." His surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, said he could fully recover in about 10 days and saw no clinical reason to cancel his Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. Doctors have not disclosed the tumor's size or whether it spread to lymph nodes, and Leo, 71, held a call with Vladimir Putin a day earlier urging a ceasefire to get supplies into Oleshky.
item.dc:creator: Joshua McElwee, Reuters

item.title: Masked settlers attack European diplomats in the occupied West Bank
item.description: Masked settlers armed with metal bars attacked Belgium's consul general, French and Polish diplomats and Catholic representatives in the West Bank Christian village of Taybeh during the olive harvest, according to Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot, who pledged to seek more EU sanctions and said "impunity for violent settlers must end." French mayor Bernard Baudoux said he was beaten and kicked despite wearing his tricolor sash, a day after an attack seriously injured a Washington Post photographer. Israel's military called it a "severe act of violence" but said the visit wasn't coordinated, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office warned against "premature conclusions" less than two weeks before national elections.
item.dc:creator: Cara Anna, Associated Press

item.title: New program looks to businesses to help fill K-3 literacy needs
item.description: The Salt Lake Chamber's Utah Rising effort has launched Literacy Match, which pairs donations from businesses, foundations and community partners with specific K-3 reading needs at schools, which then report how the money was spent. Chamber CEO Derek Miller, who said he needed reading intervention himself in second grade, pointed to 2025 data showing only 50.3% of Utah third graders read at grade level and set a goal of 100% by 2030. Early efforts include literacy nights at four high-need pilot schools and 6,000 summer reading kits assembled with the Granite Education Foundation.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Are rising ACT scores signaling COVID 'recovery' in Utah schools?
item.description: Utah's class of 2026 posted an average ACT composite of 20.1, up from 19.9 and above the 18.8 national average, ranking first among the 16 states that test more than 90% of graduates. State testing also showed year-over-year gains since the pandemic, with science proficiency at a record 49.8%, though English language arts at 45.4% and math at 42.5% remain below 2019 baselines. Fewer than half of students in grades 3-8 were proficient in reading, and math was the weakest subject for high schoolers, with 34.5% proficient on the Utah Aspire Plus test.
item.dc:creator: Jason Swensen, Deseret News

item.title: Potentially dangerous 'earth fissures' surface as a symptom of long-term aquifer depletion
item.description: Utah Geological Survey senior geologist Tyler Knudsen has been mapping earth fissures in southern Utah, cracks that can run a couple of miles long and surface after heavy rain, which he calls a symptom of aquifers being drained faster than runoff can refill them. In Enoch's Pineview Estates one crack is undermining a home's garage, and a 2.4-mile fissure killed the planned Parkview subdivision after wrecking its only house in 2009. Weber Basin Water's Darren Hess said his district has had to lower pumps as groundwater declined, while Knudsen urged users to treat water as "a finite resource" and take less of it.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: Japan's Omron to buy US industrial PC firm Onlogic for $675 million in physical AI push
item.description: Japanese manufacturer Omron will buy U.S. industrial PC maker Onlogic and its parent, Interlogic, for $675 million to build physical AI services within its industrial automation business. Omron plans to pair Onlogic's PCs with its high-precision control technology and expand in the U.S., while Onlogic keeps its brand and management as an independent business.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Hogle Zoo takes in two spider monkeys rescued from trafficking
item.description: Utah's Hogle Zoo has taken in Romina and Eve, two young spider monkeys rescued from wildlife traffickers at the border and first hand-reared at Texas' Gladys Porter Zoo, and introduced them to resident monkeys Lemon and Ebony. Associate animal care director Clair Hallyburton said Eve still clings to Romina's back for comfort and that "it's obvious these monkeys should have been with their mothers." The zoo says rising demand for baby spider monkeys fuels poaching, and it urged people to stop engaging with social media posts that portray primates as pets.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Settlement in deadly Tremonton shooting outlines payout, changes made to dispatch
item.description: A settlement obtained through a records request shows Utah's Department of Public Safety paid $700,000 to Box Elder County sheriff's Deputy Mike Allred, who was wounded in the Aug. 17, 2025, Tremonton shooting that killed Sgt. Lee Sorenson and Officer Eric Estrada, and it outlines changes made at all DPS dispatch centers. Allred, now running for Box Elder County sheriff, said he has about 200 pieces of shrapnel in his face and head and called the dispatch changes "positive," though he declined to discuss communications that night because of the pending case against suspect Ryan Michael Bate. He said his goal is to get every agency "back to one radio channel" in the county after several cities moved dispatch to Weber Area Dispatch.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: Adult acne is real, and treatable. Here's what to know
item.description: Acne can return or worsen in adulthood, with hormonal breakouts in women often showing up along the jawline and chin, and dermatologists say persistent breakouts or changes in skin color or texture merit a doctor's visit. Treatments range from benzoyl peroxide, salicylic acid and adapalene to prescription antibiotics, tretinoin, isotretinoin, birth control or spironolactone, and picking pimples worsens inflammation and scarring, especially on darker skin. Johns Hopkins dermatologist Dr. Crystal Aguh said the causes and treatments are well understood and urged people, "don't suffer alone."
item.dc:creator: Adithi Ramakrishnan, Associated Press

item.title: Utah Tech University gets $1M federal grant to research rare childhood neurological disorder
item.description: Utah Tech University received its first National Institutes of Health research grant, $1,010,605 for assistant biology professor Hung-Yu Shih to study 4H leukodystrophy, a rare childhood neurological disorder with no effective treatment. The project uses zebrafish, CRISPR genome editing and small-molecule screening to examine how defects in POLR3 genes drive the disease and to find compounds with therapeutic potential. Dean Donald Plumlee said awards at this level are usually associated with large research universities and medical centers, and undergraduate and graduate students will work on the research.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Dating app Bumble in advanced talks to go private at $1 billion valuation, source says
item.description: Bumble is in advanced talks to be taken private by Ithaca Holdings, the tech holding company of Ravi Gupta and John Hegeman, in a deal valuing the dating app at about $1 billion, a source told Reuters, sending shares up about 50% from a roughly $389 million market value. The company has been exploring a sale as Gen Z users tire of swiping; paying users fell more than 11% in 2025 to about 3.7 million and revenue slipped nearly 10% to about $966 million. CEO Whitney Wolfe Herd, who returned to the role last year, has been adding AI features to restart growth.
item.dc:creator: Milana Vinn, Reuters

item.title: Cache Valley students wear blue to honor classmates killed in carbon monoxide tragedy
item.description: Students at North Cache Middle School wore blue Monday to honor two classmates who died with three other family members in a suspected carbon monoxide poisoning in Richmond, found Saturday after a neighbor heard alarms. Three of the four children who died attended Cache County schools, and the district said it is adding counseling at affected schools. Investigators believe the deaths were accidental and have not released the victims' names.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: Utah County teen returns home after spinal cord injury, surrounded by community support
item.description: Mapleton teen Gunnar Olsen came home Monday to a crowd of family, friends and neighbors after months of hospital care and rehabilitation for a spinal cord injury he suffered diving into the ocean off California this summer. His parents say he has regained feeling in his biceps and can feel touch on his knees; the family is also facing his father Chad's stage 4 pancreatic cancer diagnosis in February. Gunnar said getting back to normal will take a long time, but urged others facing hardship to "Just keep going."
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell, KSL

item.title: New fire station election canceled on Kaysville ballots
item.description: The Kaysville City Council voted in a special meeting to pull a proposed $16.5 million bond for a second fire station from the November ballot, even though ballots were printed and many already mailed; any votes on the question will be void. Mayor Tami Tran said the city never solicited an opposing argument as a 2025 state law requires and wanted to be "overly transparent" on something so big. The city says west-side emergency responses average about eight minutes, and it expects the bond to return on the November 2027 ballot.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena and Britt Johnson, KSL

item.title: UDOT to temporarily close Guardsman Pass amid snow forecast
item.description: UDOT closed Guardsman Pass, the road linking the top of the Cottonwood Canyons with the Wasatch backcountry, at 9:30 p.m. Monday ahead of the season's first big snowfall, warning fall-color visitors to expect "winter conditions" beforehand. A foot or more could fall near the top of the Cottonwood Canyons as Tropical Storm Rachel's remnants merge with a slow-moving low, and UDOT said the closure is not the seasonal one but gave no reopening date.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Emergency help was delayed by confusion after failed execution of Christa Pike, 911 calls reveal
item.description: 911 dispatch recordings reviewed by the Associated Press show emergency help for Christa Pike was delayed by about half an hour after her failed Sept. 30 lethal injection, as responders were told at one point it was "a false call" before Tennessee prison officials confirmed the emergency at 9:11 p.m. Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital, spent time on a ventilator and has since returned to the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center. The state has not said what went wrong, though experts are examining whether a faulty IV line let the drug pool in her tissue.
item.dc:creator: Eugene Johnson, Hannah Schoenbaum and Holly Meyer, Associated Press

item.title: After nearly dying in fall from overpass, UHP trooper returns to patrol
item.description: Utah Highway Patrol trooper Steve "Odie" Myer, who fell nearly 60 feet from an I-80 overpass while laying spike strips during a February 2024 pursuit, is back on full-time patrol out of Tooele and recently recertified to ride a UHP motorcycle. The fall shattered his pelvis and tore his heart from its cavity, and after nine surgeries he credits the Department of Public Safety helicopter crew that flew him to the hospital, saying "Those guys are a miracle to me." He still faces another surgery and has worked with a therapist to revisit the overpass, but said, "As long as I can do it, I'm going to continue doing it."
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: Runners recount 'positive' experience at Moab 240-mile race despite weather cancellation
item.description: About 130 runners in the Moab 240, a 240-mile ultramarathon through the La Sal Mountains, were stopped at the remote Bridger Jack aid station after torrential rain, flash flooding and 30-mph gusts, and all were accounted for. Spanish Fork's Brian Jones, running a race named for his late brother Stephen, praised organizers' preparation but suggested a "contingency route" for emergencies. Pacer Matt Van Horn called the race positive overall but said the cold, wet night at Bridger Jack "was a test of endurance in itself."
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown and Bryanna Willis, KSL

item.title: Kroger plans to eliminate 3,000 corporate roles, memo shows, as it expands AI use
item.description: Kroger CEO Greg Foran told staff in a memo seen by Reuters that the grocer plans to eliminate roughly 3,000 corporate roles, about 37% of its 8,200 corporate employees, over three years as it builds AI into its workflows. Foran said cutting duplicative work would help lower prices and fund in-store staff, with details to come in the coming months. The owner of Utah's Smith's stores recently trimmed its sales target as it tries to compete with Walmart and Aldi, and it cut about 1,000 corporate jobs in June 2025.
item.dc:creator: Juveria Tabassum, Reuters

item.title: Police find severed tongue, still looking for victim
item.description: West Valley City police found a severed tongue on rocks after a Sept. 5 fight at an apartment complex near 1800 West and 3900 South, where a witness said five men held another man down and beat him with rocks. More than a month later the victim, believed to be a Hispanic man in his early 20s, has not been found, and no area hospital reported treating anyone for such an injury. Witnesses said the attackers, one holding a knife, fled in a red car, and no arrests have been made.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Utah's Amendment A seeks to modernize constitutional amendment publication requirements
item.description: Amendment A on Utah's November ballot would drop the statehood-era requirement that proposed constitutional amendments be printed in a newspaper in every county for two months before an election, substituting publication "in a manner provided by statute" for 60 days. Lawmakers moved after a 2024 court ruling voided Amendment D partly over that notice rule, and a companion law, HB481, would post amendment text on the state's Public Notice Website and the Legislature's site starting in 2027. The measure passed the Legislature unanimously and, unlike the tax-initiative Amendment B, has no organized opposition; Rep. Anthony Loubet said print papers are no longer "where people get their information."
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Advisory issued as remnants produce Utah's first big mountain snow of the season
item.description: Tropical Storm Rachel's remnants dropped close to 5 inches of precipitation atop the Cottonwood Canyons and Mount Timpanogos, flooding roads and pushing statewide mountain soil moisture toward a 20-year high, and the National Weather Service issued its first winter weather advisory of the season. A slow-moving low is expected to bring 2 to 6 inches of snow to most mountains through early Thursday, with up to a foot at the tops of the Cottonwood Canyons and Brian Head and 1 to 2 feet in the Uintas. KSL meteorologist Devan Masciulli called it "a beneficial storm" apart from the flash flooding, a strong start to the water year after last year's record-low snowpack.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Have You Seen This? Floods impact Utah roadways
item.description: Video from UDOT's Cottonwoods social account showed Tropical Storm Rachel's floodwaters and debris crossing state Route 190 on Sunday, closing Big Cottonwood Canyon to uphill traffic, while Carbon County deputies shared photos of flood damage and warned drivers off Nine Mile Road. The National Weather Service expects more rain Monday through Wednesday.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Meta releases Muse Wonder AI models to challenge Anthropic and OpenAI
item.description: Meta released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, billed as its most capable AI models yet, with the first set to power its Muse personal agent for subscribers and the second offered through its Muse Code coding tool; shares rose about 4%. The company said a 14-month overhaul had taken it "from rebuilding our foundations to pushing the frontier," following Mark Zuckerberg's costly push to hire researchers and close the gap with OpenAI and Anthropic.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: FBI issues actor Selma Blair a summons accusing her of assaults aboard a plane, AP source says
item.description: The FBI issued actor Selma Blair, 54, a summons alleging assaults aboard a Delta flight from Los Angeles after Port Authority police took her into custody at New York's JFK Airport over reports she was abusive and injured two flight attendants. The case will go through the petty violations court in Brooklyn federal court, and a Blair representative said a medical emergency led to the alleged conduct. Delta said it "has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior."
item.dc:creator: Michael R. Sisak, Associated Press

item.title: Hurricane Simon weakens to Category 2 as it continues to lash Mexico's Pacific coast
item.description: Hurricane Simon weakened to a Category 2 storm with 105 mph winds Monday as it churned just off Mexico's Pacific coast, where one elderly person died in Guerrero and Puerto Vallarta's airport closed until Tuesday morning. President Claudia Sheinbaum called the damage so far "minor," while officials urged residents of Jalisco, Colima, Michoacán and Nayarit to shelter and warned of storm surge. Forecasters expect more than 12 inches of rain in the hardest-hit parts of Nayarit and Sinaloa before a likely Thursday landfall, raising the risk of flash floods and landslides.
item.dc:creator: Gonzalo Zegarra, Mitchell McCluskey, Dakota Smith, Mary Gilbert, CNN

item.title: 'Severely unaffordable': Housing prices, cost of living plague Utah quality of life survey
item.description: The Utah Foundation's Community Quality of Life Index fell to 63 out of 100 in 2026, a 10-point decline since 2013 and the lowest since the survey began 15 years ago, driven mainly by housing affordability and the cost of living. "People do not feel good about the affordability of housing in their communities," said foundation president Shawn Teigen, as Utah's $559,000 median single-family home price ranks among the nation's 10 highest. Every community factor except parks and recreation and community safety declined significantly, and the report calls for targeted policy interventions.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Marijuana on the ballot for the final time in Idaho? Voters to decide if lawmakers have sole power to legalize
item.description: Idaho voters will decide in November on House Joint Resolution 4, a constitutional amendment giving the Legislature sole power to legalize marijuana, narcotics or other psychoactive substances and blocking citizen initiatives on the subject. Co-sponsor Clint Hostetler, citing what he saw as legalization's toll in California, called it a protective tool and said voters still make the final call. Southern Idaho Republican Women president Alexandra Caval countered, "We just really don't need to give up constitutional rights in order to protect ourselves from marijuana and its effects."
item.dc:creator: Lorien Nettleton, KIVI

item.title: Archbishop of the U.S. military says Catholic soldiers should not serve on firing squad
item.description: Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the Catholic Church's ministry to the U.S. military, said Catholic soldiers assigned to the Army firing squad for Nidal Hasan's Dec. 3 execution should ask to be excused, calling the duty contrary to church teaching. He also condemned plans to livestream the execution of Hasan, the Army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, asking whether exposing the public to it would "serve any purpose."
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: Pest control employee accused of stealing jewelry on a job
item.description: Eric Michael Thomas, 26, of Millcreek, was charged with second-degree felony theft after Summit County deputies say he took about $14,000 in jewelry from a home he was servicing as a pest control worker, then fished some of it out of an insecticide container in his truck. According to the affidavit, he admitted taking jewelry or small valuables from more than 10 other homes and kept the haul in a box in his desk, and a search of his home turned up more pieces. Prosecutors want him held without bail, citing his employer's report that he returns to Thailand after each season and their suspicion he meant to sell the items there.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Utahns speak their minds on AI policy: 'Learn from experts, not from lobbyists'
item.description: At the Utah Solutions Forum, a pilot citizens' assembly organized by Mormon Women for Ethical Government, 40 Utahns spent two days drafting 10 recommendations on AI and data centers, including a "dedicated information hub" backed by 95% of attendees and AI literacy classes for legislators and the public. Organizer Catherine Eslinger said AI was chosen because "people are not really in a particular partisan camp related to AI yet," and the proposals will go to city, county, school board and possibly state officials. State AI office director Zach Boyd pointed to legislative working groups and the governor's Pro-Human AI Initiative, which is weighing issues such as deepfakes, clinical AI and chatbots' effects on children.
item.dc:creator: Leah Bowers, Deseret News

item.title: Agents search Rep. Omar's Washington home in criminal probe as she vows she won't 'be silenced'
item.description: Homeland Security Investigations agents executed a court-authorized search warrant Monday at Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington-area home in a federal criminal investigation whose scope the Justice Department did not disclose. The search came three weeks before the midterms, despite the department's practice of avoiding overt steps involving candidates near an election, and followed months of claims by Vice President JD Vance and other officials that Omar committed immigration fraud, which she denies. Omar called it an "attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement" and said, "I will not be silenced."
item.dc:creator: Alanna Durkin Richer and Eric Tucker, Associated Press

item.title: Greenland lawmakers signal support for Trump security deal
item.description: Most of Greenland's lawmakers backed the island's new security agreement with the U.S. and Denmark during a parliamentary debate Monday; the deal clears the way for two new U.S. military bases and Trump's "Golden Dome" missile defense system while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' self-determination. Naleraq party chair Pele Broberg objected that Greenlanders "are not guaranteed any fixed payment" for the extensive rights granted to the U.S. Government parties, which hold a majority, defended it, with Foreign Minister Mute Egede calling it "a huge step forward," and the bill faces a second reading before a final vote.
item.dc:creator: Louise Rasmussen, Soren Jeppesen and Agnieszka Olenska, Reuters

item.title: Saturday Night Live takes aim at Kevin O'Leary, Box Elder County data center project
item.description: NBC's Saturday Night Live parodied developer Kevin O'Leary and his Stratos data center proposal in Box Elder County, with James Austin Johnson playing O'Leary on Weekend Update as unbothered by the project's noise and water effects because "I don't live there." The sketch also mocked the federal defamation suit two Utah groups filed after O'Leary suggested opponents had links to China; he has sought its dismissal. In reality, developers say they will use water-sparing technology, have cut the footprint from 40,000 to 20,000 acres and plan 1.5 gigawatts of generating capacity in a first phase.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Gathering Israel: Elder Ronald A. Rasband dedicates Ephraim Utah Temple
item.description: Elder Ronald A. Rasband of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles dedicated the Ephraim Utah Temple on Sunday, calling the site, settled by his great-great-grandparents in 1850, "sacred ground." He said a temple near Snow College gives students new chances to gather Israel, a task he tied to the tribe of Ephraim, the city's namesake, and noted his great-grandfather helped build the Manti temple 7 miles away. Announced by the late President Russell M. Nelson in 2021, the temple brings the church to 224 dedicated temples, and together the Ephraim and Manti temples need about 2,500 workers.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Bristol Myers therapy slows rare tumor progression, bolstering radiopharma push
item.description: Bristol Myers Squibb said its radiopharmaceutical RYZ101, acquired in its $4.1 billion RayzeBio takeover, significantly delayed disease progression in a late-stage trial of patients with gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors that had worsened after Lutetium-177 therapy. The drug uses the isotope actinium-225 to deliver radiation directly to tumor cells; the company said safety matched earlier studies but held back detailed data for a future medical meeting. Shares rose nearly 4% premarket as investors watch whether next-generation radiopharmaceuticals can build on Novartis' success.
item.dc:creator: Siddhi Mahatole, Reuters

item.title: Russell Brand is on trial for rape and sexual assault. His career has been a catalog of controversy
item.description: British comedian and actor Russell Brand, 51, goes on trial in London on Monday after pleading not guilty to three counts of rape, one of indecent assault and three of sexual assault involving six women, with the allegations dating to the start of his career. CNN's profile traces his rise through British TV and stand-up in the 2000s and the 2008 "Sachsgate" scandal over lewd voicemails left for actor Andrew Sachs, which ended his BBC Radio 2 show. Brand went on to Hollywood roles in "Forgetting Sarah Marshall" and "Get Him to the Greek" and a brief marriage to Katy Perry.
item.dc:creator: Amarachi Orie, CNN

item.title: Amazon in talks to buy AI startup Decart for around $7 billion, WSJ reports
item.description: Amazon is negotiating to acquire Decart, an Nvidia-backed AI startup, for roughly $7 billion, Reuters reports, citing the Wall Street Journal. Decart's Lucy model edits live video in real time, and its Oasis model builds simulated environments for training robots and self-driving systems. The company was valued at nearly $4 billion around a $300 million round in May led by Radical Ventures, and Anthropic reportedly walked away from a possible deal last month after due diligence. Neither Amazon nor Decart commented.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Utah group says there's a faster way to block Flock cameras — without legislation
item.description: Utah Civic Compact, a nonprofit that opposes automated license plate readers, wants the Utah Department of Transportation to invoke a clause in its contract with Flock Group Inc. that allows termination if the agency finds the public does not support the company's work. Spokesperson Clark Dice argued at a Friday news conference at the Capitol that UDOT acting would be quicker than waiting for lawmakers to tighten data rules, citing public anger and cases of cameras being vandalized. UDOT spokesperson John Gleason said attorneys were reviewing the contract, but that the department only handles permits and safety along state highways, cannot see the data, and leaves questions about the cameras' purpose to the police agencies that request them. Law enforcement defends the technology as a crime-solving tool, while Gov. Spencer Cox has voiced concern about officers misusing the data, Utah News Dispatch reports.
item.dc:creator: Annie Knox, Utah News Dispatch

item.title: Isaias moves north into Appalachians and mid-Atlantic; Southern California battered by Rachel
item.description: Hurricane Isaias, the Atlantic season's first, has been tied to at least four deaths in Florida and Alabama after coming ashore Friday near Destin as a Category 2 storm, and its remnants brought flooding, landslides and rescues to western North Carolina on Sunday. One station in McDowell County logged more than 9.5 inches of rain in 24 hours, while Panhandle residents lined up for supplies and fewer than 300,000 customers were still without power Sunday evening.
