On the West Coast, the remnants of Rachel, now a post-tropical cyclone, sent unusually large surf pounding Southern California, the Associated Press reports.
item.dc:creator: Sophie Bates, Kate Brumback and Julie Walker, Associated Press

item.title: Resident escapes house fire in Idaho Falls; damage estimated at $20K
item.description: A kitchen fire caused an estimated $20,000 in damage to a home on Daffodil Place on the south side of Idaho Falls on Saturday morning, according to the city. The occupant who got out told firefighters, dispatched around 7:54 a.m., that someone else might still be inside, but a search turned up no one before crews put out the flames. Investigators had not determined a cause by Saturday afternoon, EastIdahoNews.com reports.
item.dc:creator: Jordan Ormond, East Idaho News

item.title: 6 senators, including Utah Sen. Curtis, call for Trump administration to 'immediately reverse course' on Russian diesel plan
item.description: Utah Sen. John Curtis joined fellow Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski and Thom Tillis and Democrats Jeanne Shaheen and Richard Blumenthal in a Sunday statement urging the Trump administration to drop its plan to buy Russian diesel. President Donald Trump said Friday that a call with Vladimir Putin had produced a deal for millions of tons of Russian diesel to ease fuel prices, but the senators said Congress was neither consulted nor given the justification the law requires, and they pointed to a 2022 ban on Russian energy imports. Sen. John Barrasso of Wyoming defended Trump as weighing tough choices while also urging him to enforce the sanctions law Congress passed last month. Columbia University energy scholar Richard Nephew said the total volume appears smaller than a single day of U.S. diesel use, the Associated Press reports.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Freking, Associated Press

item.title: Great Salt Lake dust: A problem Utah can't afford to fix or ignore
item.description: Panelists at a Great Salt Lake Alliance event Monday weighed how Utah should handle dust from more than 800 square miles of exposed lakebed, about 70 of which University of Utah researchers classify as active hotspots. University research professor Derek Mallia called the problem urgent, while David Parrott of the Great Salt Lake Institute said the dust's makeup, including the widely assumed arsenic, remains unproven; the university puts the health toll at $116 million a year and about seven premature deaths. Bryce Bird, director of the Utah Division of Air Quality, said ozone, which has exceeded federal standards 19 times this year, is a more pressing concern than lake dust, which has yet to break an EPA limit. The speakers agreed the cheapest remedy is getting more water into the lake, pointing to the costly dust controls at California's Owens Lake, the Deseret News reports.
item.dc:creator: Leah Bowers, Deseret News

item.title: Moab 240 cut short after 70 runners and volunteers were rescued
item.description: Organizer Destination Trail called off the Moab 240 ultramarathon on Sunday, citing worsening wind, rain, freezing temperatures and damaged aid stations, after about 70 runners and volunteers were stranded Saturday night near Bridger Jack Mesa when a storm made Cottonwood Creek unsafe to cross. The nearly 242-mile race loops through country around Canyonlands and Arches national parks. Andrea Christensen, who was pacing a friend, described freezing rain, lightning and treacherous mud on an exposed climb through the Babylon Fire burn scar near Shea Mountain. She left the course at Mile 115 and said she had told her runner that no finish was worth risking anyone's safety.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: This sweet spot is plunging into fall with chocolate-covered goodness
item.description: Chocolate Plunge, a Rexburg dessert shop, has opened a second store at Hitt and Sunnyside roads in Idaho Falls. Owner Ty Walker showed off seasonal items such as a pumpkin spice hot chocolate made with Reed's Dairy pumpkin milk and chocolate-dipped pumpkin cheesecake, alongside its staple fountain-dipped strawberries with 16 topping choices. The shop also caters events and stays open until 10 p.m. on weekdays and 11 p.m. on weekends, EastIdahoNews.com reports.
item.dc:creator: Nate Eaton, East Idaho News

item.title: In Silicon Valley, AI founders cheer Trump's calls for the industry to police itself on safety
item.description: At San Francisco's Tech Week, AI founders and investors celebrated the Trump administration's hands-off approach to regulation, highlighted late last month by a voluntary 308-word safety pact for leading labs. Speakers at an Andreessen Horowitz event focused on defense opportunities, with PitchBook's Kyle Stanford noting that $13.5 billion of new defense spending is earmarked for autonomous systems and AI. Critics, including former OpenAI safety leader David Robinson, said self-policing is no substitute for law, and three OpenAI researchers posted that they had been fired. The Associated Press notes Trump repealed Biden-era AI safeguards and has moved to block state-level AI rules.
item.dc:creator: Garance Burke, Associated Press

item.title: 26-year-old Zebra in Utah seeks companionship after losing animal friends
item.description: Karen Becker of Dameron Valley in Washington County is looking for a companion, ideally a donkey on loan from a local farmer, for Zoolu, her 26-year-old Chapman zebra. Zoolu lost her last pasture mates, a Friesian horse and a Watusi bull, in recent months and now has a large field to herself. Becker received the zebra as a Christmas gift from her husband 21 years ago and went on to take in dozens of rescued exotic animals, peaking at 65 on a 20-acre farm in Morgan before moving south six years ago. She said the couple is done acquiring new animals as they near retirement but wants Zoolu to have company for the rest of her life.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Critical Minerals Agenda comes for America's 'Forgotten Wildlife Corridor'
item.description: A joint investigation by Inside Climate News and Columbia Journalism Investigations examines how the push for lithium threatens wildlife in places like the McDermitt Caldera on the Oregon-Nevada border, where the proposed McDermitt Lithium project overlaps one of the last strongholds of the sage-grouse. The bird's numbers have fallen about 80% since 1965 as sagebrush disappears, and Katie Fite of WildLands Defense said so little habitat remains that measures like seasonal drilling pauses cannot offset the damage. The reporters' database counts just one operating U.S. lithium mine, Albemarle's Silver Peak in Nevada, with at least six more expected by 2030 and many others proposed, some beside endangered species such as the buckwheat at Ioneer's Rhyolite Ridge site. The story says the Trump administration is weakening endangered-species protections while fast-tracking mine permits.
item.dc:creator: Wyatt Myskow, Inside Climate News and Johanna Hansel and Carla Samon Ros, Columbia Journalism Investigations

item.title: Where's the beef? This rancher hopes it stays in Utah
item.description: Nephi rancher Korey Wright wants Utah-raised cattle processed and eaten in Utah rather than shipped to the Big Four meatpackers, which handle roughly 85% of U.S. beef. Wright says the 2020 pandemic, when ranchers had market-ready cattle but nowhere to process them, exposed a hole in the state's food supply. His Bar-W plant in Nephi, finished in 2024 and among the first built in Utah in more than half a century, can handle about 12,000 head a year and includes a retail store. The Draper native and former Utah Highway Patrol trooper left law enforcement in 2012 to ranch full time and now runs 6,000 to 8,000 cattle, Lee Benson writes for the Deseret News.
item.dc:creator: Lee Benson, Deseret News

item.title: First Baptist Church of Salt Lake City finds 'creative uses' for historic building
item.description: The First Baptist Church of Salt Lake City at 777 S. 1300 East, dedicated in 1954, was built for more than 1,000 worshippers under Pastor Fenwick Fowler's vision of a Baptist cathedral for the city. Pastor Curtis L. Price said today's congregation is much smaller but thriving, and the church keeps the building busy with community uses ranging from Alcoholics Anonymous meetings and weddings to a samurai dojo. A former children's chapel now houses a childcare center serving about 100 kids under 5 each day. Price also traced Utah's Baptist roots to an Ogden congregation founded in 1881 and joked that the sanctuary is so large even a 4-foot Advent star looks small.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Taylorsville event gathers winter coats, Halloween costumes for families in need
item.description: The Family Support Center gave away winter coats and Halloween costumes for kids from infants to teens at its Taylorsville site Saturday, drawing more than 500 families despite the rain. Executive director Lori Cox said rising costs have left many parents unable to afford either. Another costume giveaway is planned for 4 to 8 p.m. Wednesday, Oct. 21, at the Raising Cane's in Midvale.
item.dc:creator: Allison Lyons, KSL

item.title: Trump says Russia and Ukraine reach 'energy ceasefire' but gives no details
item.description: President Donald Trump announced on social media Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate "energy ceasefire," but neither government nor the White House offered any terms. The same day, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told ABC that Kyiv would stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow ended attacks on Ukraine's power grid, and, responding to Trump's call for a new Ukrainian leader, said elections could follow a 60-day total ceasefire. A Ukrainian drone strike Sunday knocked out a Yandex data center in Vladimir, disrupting services in several countries. Trump has blamed record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine's strikes and last week struck a deal to buy Russian diesel, the Associated Press reports.
item.dc:creator: Collin Binkley, Susie Blann and Elise Morton, Associated Press

item.title: 6 people rescued from three-alarm house fire in West Valley City
item.description: Firefighters pulled three children and two adults from the basement of a burning West Valley City home early Sunday, and a third adult got out alone, according to the West Valley City Fire Department. Crews called at about 1:38 a.m. to 4671 W. Trinity Ave. found the house fully engulfed and flames spreading next door; all six occupants were hospitalized for smoke inhalation and were alert. Both houses are expected to be total losses, and the cause is under investigation, with four other fire agencies assisting.
item.dc:creator: Sicily Stanton, KSL

item.title: Man stabbed during large fight near Salt Lake City nightclub
item.description: Salt Lake City police say a man in his 20s was stabbed in the abdomen early Sunday when a crowd of more than 50 people brawled in a dirt lot near the Area 51 nightclub at 270 S. 300 West. Officers found him about a block away, and he was taken to Intermountain Medical Center in fair condition, Lt. Josh Moody said. Witnesses pointed to another man as the attacker, but the victim has not cooperated, and no suspect or arrest has been announced; police said there is no wider threat.
item.dc:creator: Sicily Stanton, KSL

item.title: Lawmakers roll out policy agenda they hope survives no matter who wins control of Congress
item.description: The Build America Caucus, a bipartisan group of about 40 House members co-chaired by Utah Rep. Celeste Maloy, released a 95-page agenda meant to guide the next Congress regardless of which party wins the midterms. The framework covers housing, permitting reform, health care, child care, infrastructure, research and education, and seeks more HUD funding and oversight to carry out the housing law passed earlier this year. Maloy told the Deseret News the plan was written by House members alone and can now be negotiated with the Senate and the Trump administration, and that its priorities reflect what she hears from Utahns worried about housing costs.
item.dc:creator: Cami Mondeaux, Deseret News

item.title: The moderate money network quietly reshaping Utah Republican politics
item.description: A cluster of center-right nonprofits formed in Utah since 2023 has become a major force in Republican politics, aiming to preserve the state's pragmatic brand of conservatism and carry it nationally, the Deseret News reports. North Carolina clean-energy philanthropist Jay Faison, who spent nearly $2.5 million backing John Curtis in 2024, gave $100,000 to Becky Edwards' Governing Group PAC and later teamed with All In For Utah founder Owen Fuller to launch what is now Doers Network. State director Zac Wilson, 31, said the group's regional advisory boards endorse candidates across the GOP spectrum based on results rather than ideology, saying he wants less drama and more legislating.
item.dc:creator: Brigham Tomco, Deseret News

item.title: From childhood poverty to life of service: Remembering Pamela Atkinson
item.description: Pamela Atkinson, the Salt Lake City advocate often called Utah's Mother Teresa for her work with homeless and low-income residents, died Saturday at 93. Born in 1933 in Bromley, England, she grew up in poverty, lived through the London Blitz and was evacuated to the countryside before education and a nursing career set her on a different path. She advised governors and other officials while also visiting people camped along the Jordan River, and she helped establish clinics serving low-income patients. A homeless medical clinic, the state's homeless trust fund and a men's resource center bear her name, the Deseret News reports.
item.dc:creator: Lois M. Collins, Deseret News

item.title: Rep. Moore acknowledges gas prices, Iran war complicate GOP economic pitch in midterms
item.description: Utah Rep. Blake Moore, the fifth-ranking House Republican, told the Deseret News he remains optimistic about the GOP's midterm prospects but acknowledged that high gas prices and the drawn-out war in Iran are overshadowing the party's record. Moore said frustration over fuel costs has eclipsed Republican gains on border security, and argued inflation was worse under President Joe Biden. He said he still opposes a nuclear-armed Iran but conceded the conflict is no longer a short-term issue and is driving up costs at home. Midterms historically punish the president's party, and the climate has shifted toward Democrats, the report notes.
item.dc:creator: Cami Mondeaux, Deseret News

item.title: Utah communities brace for Tropical Storm Rachel's rain
item.description: Utah cities are preparing for the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel, forecast to bring 1 to 3 inches of rain and gusts near 50 mph through Monday, with Sunday expected to be the wettest day. Dallan Jensen of Utah Flood Guys warned that basements and window wells are especially vulnerable, that wind can loosen shingles, and that mold can set in within days once water gets inside. Riverton Mayor Tish Buroker said the city has been readying its drainage system and continues to upgrade its stormwater standards.
item.dc:creator: Tyrese Boone, KSL

item.title: Cedar City teen riding from 'C to sea' on solo bikepacking trip to Pacific Ocean
item.description: Ollie Bryan, a 17-year-old from Cedar City, is cycling about 650 miles to the California coast on a trip he named "C to Sea," after the C on the hillside above his hometown. He set out Monday aiming for 80 miles a day and a finish next Tuesday, hauling his own food, water, tent and stove in bike bags he sewed himself, with his grandparents meeting him in the evenings. It is his second long ride after an Idaho-to-Arizona trek this summer. His father, SUU Outdoors director Derek Bryan, said the homeschooled teen planned the adventure entirely on his own.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: How do you move a 2,000-pound pumpkin? This Utahn shows us
item.description: Neurologist Mohammed Sadiq grows Atlantic Giant pumpkins in a 60-by-100-foot greenhouse, a hobby that began 17 years ago with a 100-pound pumpkin he mistakenly thought was a record. This season he won weigh-offs in Logan, with a 2,144-pound entry, and at the state fair, and planned to bring a third pumpkin to Pumpkinpalooza at the Gateway in Salt Lake City on Saturday. Sadiq said hauling the fragile giants to competitions is the nerve-wracking part, since one crack can end a season, and KSL's video report shows how he does it.
item.dc:creator: Peter Rosen, KSL

item.title: Utah needs a 'Code Red' policy to protect the homeless from extreme heat, report says
item.description: A University of Utah report released Monday recommends that lawmakers adopt a hot-weather counterpart to Utah's Code Blue cold-weather shelter expansion after studying how unsheltered people in the Salt Lake Valley cope with summer heat. Researchers interviewed 24 people, eight of whom carried GPS phones and backpack weather sensors for six days that logged repeated exposure above risk thresholds of 91 and 102.9 degrees, and they reported dehydration, heat exhaustion and lost sleep. Interviews with about 30 business staff found many storefronts serve as informal cooling spots under inconsistent, case-by-case rules that the authors said cannot replace public cooling infrastructure. Previous Code Red bills from Sen. Todd Weiler in 2025 and Rep. Steve Eliason this year both failed in the House, Utah News Dispatch reports.
item.dc:creator: Katie McKellar, Utah News Dispatch

item.title: Panama declares a state of emergency as powerful quake aftershocks rattle communities
item.description: Panama declared a state of emergency Saturday after magnitude 7.7 and 6.6 earthquakes on Friday, centered in Herrera province, were followed by more than 100 aftershocks. No deaths were reported, but officials counted 27 injuries and damage in every province, including roughly 420 homes and a similar number of schools, plus churches, hotels and bridges, with the worst in the central provinces; the colonial-era Church of San Atanasio in La Villa de Los Santos collapsed. A Mexican seismologist credited Panama's strict building codes for the comparatively low toll after deadly quakes in Venezuela and Colombia this year. The Panama Canal kept operating, while the U.S. sent a disaster team and pledged $5 million in aid, the Associated Press reports.
item.dc:creator: Aris Mariota and Alma Solis, Associated Press

item.title: Shooting leaves 9 dead, including suspect, in Erie, Pennsylvania, police say
item.description: Police in Erie, Pennsylvania, say a 45-year-old man killed eight people Friday evening at his home, including seven relatives such as a pregnant woman and young children, before killing himself. Chief Rick Lorah said two women who came to the door shortly before 5 p.m. were shot outside as they ran toward him, and officers later found six more victims and the gunman inside, among them a 5-year-old boy and a 1-year-old girl. Lorah would not discuss a motive but said investigators will examine the phones of the women killed outside, who appeared to know something was wrong. Gov. Josh Shapiro pledged state support, and District Attorney Elizabeth Hirz asked the public to avoid speculation, the Associated Press reports.
item.dc:creator: Holly Ramer and Jacqueline Ganun, Associated Press

item.title: Mortgage applications down as rates head up
item.description: Rising borrowing costs are cooling home-loan demand: the Mortgage Bankers Association reported a 4.2% weekly drop in applications for the week ending Oct. 2, with refinance applications down 8% on the week and 56% from a year earlier. Freddie Mac's average 30-year fixed rate reached 7.4%, its highest since November 2023, and MBA economist Joel Kan said the jump is pushing would-be buyers to the sidelines. Adjustable-rate mortgages, averaging about 6.43% for a five-year initial term, have climbed to just over 10% of applications. Realtor.com economist Hannah Jones said ARMs may be the only entry point for some buyers but warned borrowers to test whether their budgets could handle a reset, recalling the payment shocks of the 2008 crisis.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Riley Roche, Deseret News

item.title: Attack on Riyadh airport killed 12 people and wounded over 300 more, Saudi authorities say
item.description: Saudi civil aviation authorities said a Saturday attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport killed 12 people, among them four Saudis and one U.S. citizen, and injured more than 300, the deadliest strike on a Gulf Arab state since the Iran war began. A regional official said a missile hit the complex for domestic terminals 3 and 4; no group immediately claimed it, though attacks on Saudi targets have surged since a Saudi-led offensive against Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels started a week ago. President Donald Trump said the U.S. was weighing whether to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis. Flights were suspended and diverted, several Western governments told citizens to avoid the airport, and airlines including Lufthansa Group and FlyDubai had already paused Saudi service, the Associated Press reports.
item.dc:creator: Samy Magdy and Cara Anna, Associated Press

item.title: 5 dead in apparent carbon monoxide poisoning incident in Cache County
item.description: A man believed to be 43 and four young people ages 5 to 16 were found dead Saturday afternoon at a Richmond apartment complex in what the Cache County Sheriff's Office called an apparent carbon monoxide poisoning. Neighbors went into the unit around 12:15 p.m. after its carbon monoxide alarms had sounded for a long time and found the man in the garage; responders then located the other four victims. Sheriff D. Chad Jensen said neighboring units were evacuated and one other man was taken to a hospital for possible exposure, and the investigation is continuing.
item.dc:creator: Alex Tumalip, KSL

item.title: 4 dead from storm as Isaias brings threat of floods across the Southeast
item.description: Isaias, the Atlantic season's first hurricane, made landfall Friday near Destin, Florida, as a Category 2 storm, tearing roofs and facades off buildings along the Panhandle before weakening to a post-tropical cyclone as it moved inland. At least four deaths were blamed on it, including people killed by falling trees in Florida and Birmingham, Alabama, a man poisoned by generator exhaust in his garage, and a crash involving a downed tree in Barbour County, Alabama. Nearly 700,000 customers lost power, and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis warned that flood danger would persist as forecasters projected heavy rain into Georgia, the Carolinas and the southern Appalachians. The Energy Department authorized emergency crude exchanges from the strategic petroleum reserve, the Associated Press reports.
item.dc:creator: Emilie Megnien, Gerald Herbert and Michael Casey, Associated Press

item.title: Historic Widowmaker hill climb in Draper gets recognition
item.description: Draper's Historic Preservation Commission has placed a marker at the Salt Lake County Flight Park honoring the Widowmaker motorcycle hill climb, a competition run by the Bee's Motorcycle Club on the steep slope from 1964 to 1988. The sign lists past champions, among them 89-year-old Mel Kimball Sr. and his son Mel Kimball Jr., who recalled years of marking the course, cleaning up and reseeding the hill, and fields of as many as 600 riders. Kimball Sr. credits a rider named Bob Ross with naming the hill after sizing it up from below. Commissioner Jason Wiggins said motorsports are now barred there but the history deserved a permanent spot, and the city planned a public commemoration Saturday morning with former racers attending.
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: Man trespassed from church property after lewdness display
item.description: Mitchell Dean Anderson, 37, has been barred from Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints properties unless he gets written permission, as part of a plea deal stemming from an incident at Temple Square during April's general conference. Prosecutors say he stripped fully naked in front of a large crowd before a church security officer covered him with a blanket and police arrested him. On Sept. 18 in 3rd District Court he pleaded guilty to class B misdemeanor lewdness under a plea in abeyance, which requires 18 months without new offenses, mental health and substance abuse evaluations with any recommended treatment, and a $200 fee in exchange for a possible reduced conviction.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Axe from 'The Shining' and other props from Stanley Kubrick's archive up for auction
item.description: Bonhams will auction pieces from director Stanley Kubrick's personal archive in London in February, after a free public exhibition. The most valuable lot is expected to be the glowing "Star Child" fetus prop from the end of "2001: A Space Odyssey," estimated at up to about $1.06 million, while Jack Nicholson's axe from "The Shining" carries an estimate of roughly $40,000 to $66,000. Other items include Kubrick's director's chair, the twin sisters' blue dresses from "The Shining," "Eyes Wide Shut" costumes and his annotated scripts. His stepdaughter Katherina Kubrick said the family hopes the pieces find owners who will cherish them, the Associated Press reports.
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: New Grantsville billboard installed to reflect city's history
item.description: Roadside muralist John Cerney, known around the country for his giant cut-out figures, has added a Utah piece inspired by the salt flats that puzzled and fascinated him on a childhood drive through the state. Titled "Salt & Pepper," the westbound I-80 billboard near Grantsville's exit 84 portrays 5-year-old Molly McShane scooping salt into a shaker. Project chairman Steve McShane said the subject ties the site to local history and to the nearby Morton Salt plant.
item.dc:creator: Allison Lyons, KSL

item.title: Public Lands department builds a prickly defense against erosion in Salt Lake City's foothills
item.description: Salt Lake City's Department of Public Lands is replanting the foothills above Red Butte Garden that were burned in the Bonneville Fire, aiming to hold soil in place before rain and to restore habitat used by a large elk herd. Restoration ecology supervisor Blake Wellard said crews put in 1,500 prickly pear cacti last week, chosen because their wide, shallow roots grip dry, rocky slopes and their flowers and edible fruit feed pollinators and other wildlife. University of Utah Greek Life volunteers are helping, and sagebrush grown by inmates in a Utah Department of Corrections greenhouse program is also going into the burn scar. The city plans more volunteer events focused on wildfire mitigation in the coming weeks.
item.dc:creator: Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: Christa Pike is discharged from a hospital after surviving execution attempt, her attorneys say
item.description: Christa Pike, 50, has left the hospital and returned to Tennessee's Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she will keep receiving care, her attorneys said Saturday. Tennessee tried to execute her Sept. 30 for the 1995 killing of classmate Colleen Slemmer, but she survived two doses of pentobarbital, at one point needing a ventilator; the Death Penalty Information Center says she is the first person known to survive receiving lethal injection drugs. The state has not explained the failure, though experts and her lawyers point to an improperly placed IV line. Gov. Bill Lee postponed the state's other scheduled execution and ordered a review, and the prison chief has resigned, the Associated Press reports.
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: Pope Leo declares death penalty 'inadmissible' as his native US plans to livestream execution
item.description: Marking the World Day Against the Death Penalty on Saturday, Pope Leo XIV used his @Pontifex account on X to restate the church's position, revised by Pope Francis in 2018, that capital punishment is inadmissible because it violates human dignity. The post did not name any case, but it came days after the U.S. Defense Department said it would livestream the Dec. 3 firing-squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of the 2009 Fort Hood shooting that killed 13. Hours earlier, Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin called making a spectacle of an execution unacceptable, and U.S. bishops' conference president Archbishop Paul Coakley urged the Pentagon to reconsider, the Associated Press reports.
item.dc:creator: Nicole Winfield, Associated Press

item.title: Filmmaker touts futuristic 'My Name Is Ringo' ahead of Provo festival stop
item.description: Jon Peter Lewis, a former "American Idol" and "The Voice" contestant who soured on the music business and later studied film at USC, will screen his short "My Name Is Ringo" at Provo's FilmQuest festival later this month. Unlike his earlier live-action work, the short was assembled in a video game engine with motion-capture performances, and Lewis taught himself the software along the way, putting in roughly 12-hour days for about 16 months. The story imagines a girl living in a future where people and robots coexist, which Lewis frames as a hopeful counterpoint to current anxieties about artificial intelligence. The screening takes place at Provo's Velour Live Music Gallery, where he spent years performing, and he hopes to grow the short into a series.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena and Diana Jones, KSL

item.title: The biggest hurdles in Western wildfires could be before and after the blaze
item.description: At a Western Wildfire Resilience Roundtable hosted Friday by the University of Utah's Wilkes Center for Climate Science and Policy, specialists argued that the largest gaps in wildfire policy lie in prevention and recovery rather than firefighting itself. Sen. John Curtis pointed to bipartisan momentum on forest management, including his Senate-passed Wildfire Emissions Prevention Act easing prescribed burns, while House Majority Leader Casey Snider described Utah's fee-funded program for homes in the wildland-urban interface, where the state counts nearly 60,000 high-risk structures. State forestry officials from Utah and Wyoming said research on post-fire erosion control and reseeding is lacking, citing destructive flooding after this year's Cottonwood Fire near Beaver. Participants agreed that data and funding remain the main constraints after a season in which more than 1,200 Utah fires burned over 560,000 acres, KSL's Carter Williams reports.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: New initiative 'Community Quest' aims to encourage exploration of Utah's diverse communities
item.description: The Utah Division of Multicultural Affairs, through its Magnify Utah initiative, launched Community Quest this summer to nudge residents toward cultural celebrations, neighborhoods and businesses outside their usual orbit. Its centerpiece is a free red "passport" booklet, printed in about 10,000 copies and stocked at many libraries, with profiles of Latino, Asian, Pacific Islander, Native American, European and Black communities as well as pioneer heritage and rural Utah. The booklet lists 55 restaurants, museums and other stops, links via QR codes to 670 more, and includes food suggestions and family-friendly games. Program manager Dustin Khong said the goal is to show that every group, rural and pioneer communities included, has traditions worth sharing.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: 2 hospitalized in Sardine Canyon collision
item.description: One person was flown to a hospital in critical condition and a second went by ambulance after a crash Friday afternoon in Sardine Canyon near Wellsville in Cache County. According to Utah Highway Patrol agent Kyley Tobler, a pickup pulling out of a mine near mile marker 11 crossed in front of a semi-truck, causing the collision.
item.dc:creator: Payton Davis, KSL

item.title: Sandy residents prepare with sandbags ahead of Rachel's remnants
item.description: Sandy homeowners hit by flooding in an August storm, including Travis Mangrum, whose basement took on water through a window well, are filling sandbags ahead of the remnants of Hurricane Rachel, forecast to bring one to three inches of rain and gusts possibly above 50 mph. The city is offering empty bags and sand near 9800 South and Highland Drive, where public works manager Scott Ellis said about 50,000 of 60,000 pounds of sand had already been used, with more due Saturday morning. Crews are also clearing storm drain inlets and staging pumps and generators. Officials described the steps as precautionary, saying major flooding was not expected though local effects were hard to predict.
item.dc:creator: Tyrese Boone, KSL

item.title: Provo school officials debate future of dual-language programming, prompting concern from some
item.description: The Provo School District is weighing changes to its dual-language immersion program, now offered at five elementary schools in Spanish, French, Portuguese and Mandarin, though spokesman Caleb Price said the board does not intend to end it outright. Options include keeping programs in neighborhood schools, consolidating into one or more magnet schools, trimming the number of languages, or expanding Spanish immersion where many students are native Spanish speakers. A committee of parents and staff, a family survey and focus groups will inform a board decision that could come in December or January, as part of a wider look at enrollment and school boundaries. Timpview High students Kate Strong and Jasmina George, both Mandarin program alumni, said the experience broadened their outlook and that younger students should keep the chance.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Why Sen. John Curtis says Utahns should care about global health
item.description: Speaking at a University of Utah global health panel on Friday, Sen. John Curtis argued that the United States still has a stake in health abroad, noting that about 500,000 Utah jobs and some $27 billion in annual trade tie the state to the world economy. The Republican said Congress is resisting attempts to claw back already-appropriated aid, but he cautioned that a national debt above $40 trillion requires tighter targeting of foreign spending, likening aid requests to employees seeking raises from a company that must stay solvent. He singled out PEPFAR, the HIV/AIDS program, as an unusually effective investment. Former Rep. Chris Stewart, who joined him at a private meeting with health leaders, said philanthropy and federal dollars are both needed and that foreign aid is a small slice of the budget, though it should have guardrails.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Pioneer Park upgrades nearing completion, with reopening set for November
item.description: Salt Lake City's renovation of Pioneer Park, underway since March, is 80% to 90% finished, and the city has scheduled a public grand reopening for Nov. 13 from noon to 2 p.m. Nancy Monteith, a senior landscape architect with the city's Public Lands department, said the park will gain six pickleball courts, a basketball court, a playground, a better off-leash dog area, a covered pavilion, room for eight food trucks and 150 new trees. A new restroom building will double as an office for three park rangers, part of an effort to make the park feel safer through daily staffing. KSL's Emma Benson reports the south end, home to the Saturday farmers market, stayed open throughout construction.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: Utah Honey Harvest Festival kicks off 14th year in Grantsville
item.description: Clark Historic Farm in Grantsville is hosting the 14th annual Utah Honey Harvest Festival this weekend, with honey tastings, beekeeping demonstrations, vendors from across Utah and fiddle music. Founder Laurie Hurst and farm director Sidney Rasher said the event draws visitors from around the region. Admission is $5, or $7 for both days, and children under 4 get in free. KSL's Joe R. Wirthlin Jr. reports Friday's schedule honored local women 75 and older as Honorary Queen Bees, while Saturday brings a honey contest for Utah beekeepers and the Sweet Fiddlin' Fest.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Davis County police shooting hospitalizes 1 person
item.description: A person was flown by Life Flight helicopter to a hospital Friday afternoon after shots were fired as a tactical team confronted a domestic violence suspect in Davis County. Clearview Police Assistant Chief Devin Rogers said the case began with a 9 a.m. report that the man had used a gun to coerce the victim, and that he was later found at a home, would not communicate with officers and had threatened violence if police got involved. Neighbors were told to shelter in place or leave before the gunfire. KSL's Joe R. Wirthlin Jr. reports officials had not said whether police, the suspect or both fired.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Once near extinction, these giant tortoises now outnumber people in the Seychelles, survey finds
item.description: An estimated 180,000 Aldabra giant tortoises now live on Aldabra Atoll in the Seychelles, the highest count ever recorded and more than the island nation's roughly 122,000 people. The figure comes from a Seychelles Islands Foundation and University of Exeter analysis of counts taken from 2018 to 2022, updating a late-1990s estimate of about 100,000. Nineteenth-century exploitation once cut the population below 1,000 before the atoll was protected in 1981 and named a UNESCO World Heritage site. Co-author Nancy Bunbury and foundation CEO Frauke Fleischer-Dogley hailed the conservation success, though researchers warn droughts and sea-level rise remain threats, CNN's Kathleen Magramo reports.
item.dc:creator: Kathleen Magramo, CNN

item.title: USU researchers study wildfire burn scars and lingering dangers
item.description: Utah State University hydrologists at the Utah Water Research Laboratory in Logan are studying how wildfire burn scars change soil and vegetation and alter how rain moves through watersheds. Associate professor Belize Lane, who leads the work, said the team measures how quickly water soaks into burned ground to estimate what storm could trigger flash floods or debris flows and how much sediment might wash downhill. She said such hazards can persist for five years or more as a watershed recovers, and the findings could guide evacuation routes and flood mitigation. KSL's Todd Kunz reports the research, previously done in Colorado and California, has moved closer to home after Utah's busy fire season.
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: Logan man who kidnapped child, requested ransom pleads guilty to assault
item.description: Renan A. Alvarez, 50, of Logan pleaded guilty Sept. 28 to aggravated assault, domestic violence in the presence of a child, property damage and drug possession in a July case that also involved taking an infant. Charges say he twice strangled a woman during an argument at home on July 8 while an 8-year-old watched, smashed her phone as she called 911, then took her 11-month-old from a stroller and drove off. About three weeks later he allegedly demanded $6,000 through his sister to return the baby, and police arrested him at the exchange after the woman paid and recovered the child. KSL's Cassidy Wixom reports prosecutors dropped both aggravated kidnapping counts and other charges and will recommend no prison time, with sentencing on Nov. 9.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Flood watches, wind advisories issued throughout Utah ahead of Rachel's arrival
item.description: The National Weather Service posted flood watches and wind advisories across Utah ahead of the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel, forecasting 1 to 2 inches of rain in most valleys and 2 to 4 inches possible from late Saturday through Monday. Flash flooding is expected Sunday in southern Utah's parks and recreation areas, and isolated mountain slopes in southwest Utah, the Book Cliffs and the Bear River Range could see 6 to 8 inches. Gusts of 55 to 60 mph are possible, and a sting jet in southwest Utah on Sunday could push winds past 70 mph, toppling trees in saturated soil, with isolated tornadoes also possible. KSL meteorologist Devan Masciulli told reporter Carter Williams totals depend on the storm's exact track and a second Pacific system arriving behind it.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Trump strikes deal with Putin for diesel in sharp reversal of US policy weeks before midterms
item.description: President Donald Trump announced Friday that Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed in a phone call to send millions of tons of diesel to the United States, starting with more than 300,000 tons immediately, a move aimed at high fuel prices before the midterms. The deal cuts against a Russia sanctions law Trump signed a month ago, and the Treasury quickly issued a license exempting loaded Russian diesel from sanctions until April 2027. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it a weak decision that would prolong the war, and Democrats including Chuck Schumer and Richard Blumenthal called it a betrayal of Ukraine. The Associated Press's Michelle L. Price and Collin Binkley report energy analysts expect little effect on U.S. diesel prices, which average $6.28 a gallon, while Russia gains a buyer for surplus summer-grade fuel.
item.dc:creator: Michelle L. Price and Collin Binkley, Associated Press
